p79: 79.  The Government submitted that the terms and expressions contained in the dictionaries concerned were based on historical and sociological facts and did not reflect any intention to debase the Roma community. They added that the Ministry of Culture had contributed financially to the publication of the dictionaries in 1991 and 1998, in a total amount of EUR 2,700. They stressed that the dictionary for pupils was not a school textbook and had been neither distributed in schools nor recommended by the Ministry of Education as a reference book for school curricula. Lastly, they observed that the impugned dictionaries had not been reprinted and were currently out of print.
p80: 80.  The Chamber had particular regard to the fact that the impugned definitions were preceded by the observation that the terms in question were used in a “metaphorical” sense. It therefore considered that these expressions had not undermined the applicant’s ethnic identity and concluded that there had been no violation of Article 8 of the Convention.
p81: 81.  The Court notes at the outset that the applicant claimed to be the victim of negative stereotyping on account of certain entries in the dictionaries in question. Article 8 of the Convention is therefore applicable for the reasons set out in paragraph 60 above. The Court further observes that, although the publication of the dictionaries was partly funded by the Ministry of Culture, the applicant brought civil proceedings solely against the Language Association, a non-governmental organisation, and did not seek to bring proceedings against the Ministry in the domestic administrative courts (see paragraphs 31-34 above). Accordingly, as with application no. 4149/04 (see paragraphs 60-61 above), the Court will examine, in the light of the general principles set out in paragraphs 62-68 above, whether the Government complied with their positive obligation under Article 8 to protect the applicant’s private life from alleged interference by a third party, in this case the Language Association.
p82: 82.  In dismissing the applicant’s claim, the Ankara Civil Court of First Instance (*tribunal de grande instance d’Ankara*) observed that the definitions and expressions in the dictionaries were based on historical and sociological reality and did not reflect any intention to humiliate or debase the Roma community. It also noted that the Turkish language contained similar expressions concerning other ethnic groups, which appeared in dictionaries and encyclopaedias (see paragraph 33 above).
p83: 83.  It thus examined the impugned entries in order to determine whether they unlawfully infringed the applicant’s rights under Article 8 of the Convention. In so doing, it applied the principles embodied in the Court’s case-law (see paragraph 66 above).
p84: 84.  In this connection, the Court observes that a dictionary is a source of information which lists the words of a language and gives their various meanings, the basic meaning being simply descriptive or literal, while others may be figurative, allegorical or metaphorical. In that sense it reflects the language used in society. In both dictionaries, the literal definition of the term “çingene” (“Gypsy”) appears on page 279. The dictionaries were thus clearly voluminous and sought to cover the entire Turkish language. The Court also notes the definition of the term “Gypsy” which appears first in the dictionaries in question and which reads as follows: “An ethnic group originating from India, whose members lead a nomadic life and have spread widely throughout the world, or a person belonging to that ethnic group.” Secondly, it is stated that, in a metaphorical sense, the term “Gypsy” also means “stingy” (see paragraph 28 above). On the same page of the dictionaries there are other definitions of certain expressions relating to Gypsies, such as “Gypsy money” and “Gypsy rose”. The Court notes in this connection that, as explained by the Ankara Civil Court of First Instance (*tribunal de grande instance d’Ankara*), these expressions form part of everyday language.
